title: Watkins & Son v. Carrig
summary: The court enforced a voluntarily agreed higher excavation price even though the original contract already required removal of the rock.

sections.Parties: Watkins & Son was the excavation contractor. Carrig was the owner who promised an increased price after rock was encountered.
sections.Material Facts:
The parties’ written contract set a price for excavating a cellar and required removal of all material. The contractor did not investigate the subsurface conditions, ask about rock, or reserve a right to a higher price for unexpected conditions. There was no finding that the owner misled it. Soon after work began, solid rock was encountered. The parties met and orally agreed on a rock-removal unit price about nine times the unit price on which the original total had been calculated. Rock ultimately occupied about two-thirds of the excavation. The contractor proceeded with the work on the strength of the new promise.

The court treated the increased price as fair compensation for the rock work. Although the contractor pressed for relief from a burdensome obligation, the owner yielded without protest and voluntarily surrendered the right to insist on the original price.
sections.Procedural History: A referee found that the oral agreement superseded the written contract and reported a verdict for the contractor. The owner excepted to acceptance of the report and entry of judgment. The New Hampshire Supreme Court overruled the exceptions.
sections.Issue: Could the price adjustment be enforced although the original contract already placed the burden of excavating rock on the contractor?
sections.Holding: Yes. The court treated the owner’s voluntary relinquishment of his existing price right and the parties’ new arrangement as effective.
sections.Reasoning:
The contractor had no mutual-mistake defense to the original obligation. It had agreed to excavate the space regardless of the material found and had assumed the risk of an unfavorable subsurface condition. The enforceability of the later agreement therefore required a separate explanation.

The court rejected an insistence that rescission and replacement occur as two temporally distinct transactions. A modification can contain a partial discharge of the old obligation. Here the owner intentionally yielded the right to require rock removal at the original price, received reasonable value under the new agreement, and allowed the contractor to proceed in reliance on that arrangement. The court emphasized the practical ability of contracting parties to adjust obligations when circumstances prove burdensome.

The result depends on this court’s treatment of a voluntary and fair adjustment. Calling a change a rescission does not automatically answer the consideration question in every jurisdiction. The comparison with Alaska Packers asks whether the owner truly consented to a reasonable adjustment or was subjected to pressure that the law should refuse to enforce.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It supplies a contrasting judicial response to the pre-existing-duty rule and makes the distinction between an assumed original risk and an enforceable later adjustment explicit.

topics.modification: The later agreement was enforced through voluntary discharge and adjustment of the existing obligation.
topics.consideration: The opinion resists a rigid application of the pre-existing-duty rule.
topics.duress: Voluntary surrender and fair value distinguish the court’s account from opportunistic coercion.
topics.mistake: The original allocation of excavation risk defeated a mistake argument.
topics.assent: The owner’s intentional agreement to the new arrangement carries the reasoning.
